articles.title: Perilous Future of the Republic
articles.author: Peter McLaren
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. American democracy is confronting a crisis that extends far beyond the personality, policies, or political ambitions of any single president. What is at stake is the historical meaning of democracy itself: whether a republic founded upon the promise of popular sovereignty can survive the concentration of executive power, the systematic weakening of institutional restraints, the mobilization of political resentment, and the transformation of public life into an arena of permanent ideological warfare. Donald Trump represents the culmination of political tendencies that have been developing within American society for decades. His presidency did not create every contradiction now confronting the republic. Rather, it has brought those contradictions into sharper relief, exposing the vulnerabilities of institutions that many Americans had assumed to be more resilient than they are. The danger is not simply that an individual president may violate democratic norms. It is that the erosion of those norms may become normalized, that the exceptional may become routine, and that the public may gradually lose the capacity to distinguish democratic government from the increasingly personalized exercise of political power. Democracy rarely disappears in a single dramatic moment. Its institutions may remain standing while their substance is hollowed out. Elections continue, courts convene, legislatures assemble, and constitutions remain ceremonially invoked. Yet the conditions necessary for meaningful democratic participation can deteriorate beneath this institutional surface. Citizens may retain the formal right to vote while losing confidence that their voices can influence the decisions shaping their lives. The question confronting the United States is therefore not merely whether its democratic institutions can withstand another political crisis. It is whether the republic can recover the social, ethical, and political commitments that make democracy something more than a procedural arrangement. The Republic at the Edge The American republic was born amid contradictions that have never been fully resolved. Its founding declarations affirmed liberty and equality while slavery remained entrenched in its economic and political foundations. The language of universal rights coexisted with the exclusion of women, Indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans, and those without property from the privileges of citizenship. These contradictions do not invalidate the democratic aspirations expressed in the founding documents. They reveal, rather, that democratic ideals have always exceeded the political arrangements through which they were initially articulated. The struggle for democracy has consequently involved generations of movements attempting to enlarge the meaning of freedom and extend the boundaries of political membership. The abolitionist movement, the labor movement, the women's suffrage movement, the civil rights movement, and countless struggles for economic justice have challenged the tendency of political institutions to serve the interests of established power. Democracy has advanced not simply because political elites voluntarily surrendered their privileges but because ordinary people organized to demand recognition, representation, and material change. This history matters because democracy cannot be reduced to reverence for national symbols or nostalgic appeals to an imagined golden age. A democratic republic is not democratic merely because it possesses a constitution, holds elections, or celebrates its founding documents. It must continually confront the inequalities and exclusions that undermine the promises those documents contain. The contemporary crisis emerges from the widening distance between democratic rhetoric and lived experience. Economic insecurity, declining trust in public institutions, political polarization, and the increasing influence of concentrated wealth have created conditions in which authoritarian appeals can acquire considerable force. For many Americans, political institutions appear remote, unresponsive, and incapable of addressing the difficulties of everyday life. Workers struggle to secure housing, healthcare, education, and economic stability while enormous concentrations of wealth accumulate beyond their reach. Communities experience the consequences of industrial decline, environmental destruction, and the erosion of public services. Political leaders promise renewal, yet the structures generating insecurity often remain largely intact. Authoritarian movements exploit this disillusionment. They identify enemies, promise national restoration, and present concentrated leadership as the remedy for political paralysis. They offer emotionally satisfying explanations for complicated social problems while directing public anger toward vulnerable populations, immigrants, political opponents, and supposedly disloyal citizens. The resulting politics transforms legitimate grievances into instruments of domination. The problem is not that ordinary people are incapable of democratic judgment. It is that democratic judgment becomes more difficult when public discourse is saturated with disinformation, fear, scapegoating, and the deliberate destruction of a shared factual world. A republic cannot remain healthy when citizens are encouraged to regard one another as existential enemies. Related: Elbows Up! Canada, Trump, and the Politics of Democratic Friendship The Imperial Presidency The American presidency has accumulated extraordinary power over the course of the nation's history. War, national security, emergency declarations, executive orders, and the expansion of administrative authority have progressively enlarged the reach of the executive branch. These developments did not begin with Trump. They reflect a longer transformation in American political life, one in which successive administrations have expanded presidential authority while Congress has frequently struggled to exercise meaningful oversight. Trump's approach to the presidency intensifies this historical tendency by treating executive power not simply as a constitutional responsibility but as an instrument of personal authority. The distinction is fundamental. A democratic president occupies an office whose legitimacy depends upon constitutional limitations, institutional accountability, and the recognition that political authority is temporary. An authoritarian leader increasingly treats those limitations as obstacles to be overcome and public institutions as instruments to be brought under personal control. Under this conception of leadership, loyalty to the president can become more important than fidelity to the law. Independent officials may be treated as enemies. Investigations may be represented as conspiracies. Judicial decisions may be denounced whenever they frustrate executive objectives. The public service itself may be reorganized around political obedience rather than professional independence. Such developments threaten the distinction between a constitutional republic and a system in which power is exercised according to the preferences of an individual leader. The danger is compounded when the president's political movement portrays any institutional resistance as illegitimate. If courts, legislatures, journalists, civil servants, and election administrators are discredited whenever they refuse to comply with executive demands, the very mechanisms designed to restrain arbitrary power become targets of political warfare. The constitutional separation of powers is not an inconvenience imposed upon effective government. It is one of the essential safeguards against the concentration of power. The founders understood that political authority requires limits because no individual, however persuasive or popular, can be presumed immune to ambition, self-interest, or the temptation to govern without restraint. The imperial presidency emerges when those limits are progressively weakened and the executive begins to behave as though the state belongs to its occupant. From Democratic Erosion to Competitive Authoritarianism Political scientists have used the concept of competitive authoritarianism to describe systems in which elections and democratic institutions continue to exist while incumbents manipulate the political environment to make genuine competition increasingly unequal. Such systems do not necessarily abolish elections. They may instead weaken the institutions that make elections meaningful: independent courts, a free press, impartial electoral administration, legislative oversight, and the ability of opposition parties to organize without intimidation. The danger for the United States is not that every feature of such systems has already become fully established. It is that democratic erosion can occur incrementally, through the cumulative weakening of safeguards that once appeared secure. An election is not sufficient to guarantee democracy. Electoral legitimacy depends upon the conditions under which political competition takes place. Citizens must be able to obtain reliable information, criticize those in power, organize collectively, and participate without fear that the machinery of government will be weaponized against them. When political leaders delegitimize electoral outcomes without credible evidence, undermine confidence in election administration, or portray political opponents as enemies of the nation, they weaken the shared commitments upon which peaceful transfers of power depend. The events surrounding January 6, 2021, demonstrated how profoundly dangerous the rejection of electoral legitimacy can become. The attack on the United States Capitol was not merely an eruption of public disorder. It was an assault upon the constitutional process through which electoral outcomes are formally recognized. The broader lesson is that democratic institutions cannot survive indefinitely when political leaders cultivate the belief that elections are legitimate only when their own side wins. Nor can democracy thrive when the public sphere becomes so saturated with conspiracy theories that evidence itself loses its authority. A political culture in which every inconvenient fact is dismissed as fabricated, every investigation is treated as persecution, and every institutional restraint is described as treason becomes increasingly incapable of resolving conflict through democratic means. The challenge is not simply to defend existing institutions. It is to restore the public trust and political culture that allow those institutions to function. Related: Che Guevara, Paulo Freire, Cuba, and the Future of Hope The Assault on Institutional Independence Democratic government requires institutions capable of exercising their responsibilities without being subordinated to the personal interests of political leaders. Courts must be able to interpret the law independently. Legislatures must be able to investigate executive conduct. Journalists must be free to scrutinize those who exercise power. Election officials must be able to administer elections without intimidation. Civil servants must be able to carry out lawful responsibilities without being forced to demonstrate personal allegiance to the president. These institutions are imperfect. They can reproduce class privilege, racial inequality, bureaucratic inertia, and other forms of injustice. Their independence does not make them immune from criticism or reform. Nevertheless, institutional independence remains essential to preventing the arbitrary exercise of political authority. The effort to subordinate public institutions to executive power represents a particularly dangerous development because it can transform the instruments of government into mechanisms of political retaliation. When public officials are threatened for performing their duties, when professional expertise is dismissed as ideological disloyalty, and when investigations are treated as unacceptable merely because they inconvenience those in power, the distinction between public service and personal obedience begins to collapse. This transformation has implications extending well beyond Washington. Universities, public schools, scientific institutions, cultural organizations, and independent media all depend upon some degree of intellectual freedom and institutional autonomy. They require the ability to examine evidence, challenge established assumptions and communicate conclusions without fear of political punishment. A society that systematically intimidates its intellectual and cultural institutions impoverishes its capacity for democratic self-understanding. The purpose of education is not to produce citizens who repeat the preferred language of those who govern them. It is to cultivate the capacity to question authority, evaluate evidence, recognize injustice, and participate thoughtfully in collective life. When these capacities are weakened, political obedience can be mistaken for civic responsibility. The defense of institutional independence must therefore be accompanied by a deeper commitment to democratic education. The Politics of Enemies Authoritarian politics depends upon the construction of enemies. Rather than acknowledging the complexity of social problems, authoritarian leaders offer narratives that divide the population into morally opposed camps. One group is presented as the authentic nation; the other is portrayed as corrupt, dangerous, parasitic, or fundamentally alien. The political leader then assumes the role of defender, promising to restore the nation by defeating those supposedly responsible for its decline. This strategy converts political disagreement into a struggle over national identity. Opponents are no longer people with different interpretations of the common good. They become enemies whose very presence is said to threaten the survival of the country. The rhetoric of national restoration can be particularly effective during periods of economic insecurity and social change. It offers a simplified account of suffering, directing anger toward identifiable targets rather than examining the economic and institutional arrangements that generate insecurity. Immigrants may be blamed for problems rooted in labor-market structures, inadequate housing, or failures of public policy. Minority populations may be portrayed as threats to social cohesion. Journalists and academics may be accused of undermining the nation simply because they challenge prevailing political narratives. Meanwhile, the power of corporations, the concentration of wealth, and the structural inequalities shaping everyday life may receive far less scrutiny. This is one of the central achievements of reactionary politics: it can mobilize genuine grievances while redirecting them away from the institutions and economic relationships that deserve critical examination. Democratic politics requires a different response. It must recognize the legitimate suffering of people whose lives have been destabilized by economic change, declining public services, and the erosion of community. Yet it must refuse the proposition that the suffering of one group can be remedied through the humiliation or exclusion of another. Solidarity does not require pretending that social conflicts do not exist. It requires understanding how those conflicts are produced and identifying possibilities for collective action that do not depend upon scapegoating. A democratic society must resist the temptation to confuse the politics of vengeance with the pursuit of justice. Related: Revolutionary Prophetic Pedagogy: Reclaiming Schools for Democracy in an Age of Oligarchy The Machinery of Power Political authority in contemporary America cannot be understood solely through the personalities of elected officials. It must also be examined in relation to the economic structures that shape the possibilities of political action. Corporate wealth, financial power, lobbying, campaign financing, media ownership, and the increasing influence of private interests over public policy all affect the conditions under which democracy operates. The formal principle of political equality becomes increasingly fragile when economic inequality translates into unequal political influence. A citizen with limited resources may possess the same legal right to vote as a billionaire, yet the two do not possess comparable opportunities to shape public debate, influence legislation, or establish the boundaries of politically acceptable discussion. This is not simply a matter of individual wealth. It concerns the institutional arrangements through which economic power becomes political power. The concentration of wealth can weaken democracy even when elections remain competitive. It can restrict the range of policies considered realistic, privilege the interests of investors over those of workers, and encourage governments to treat the demands of financial markets as more urgent than the needs of ordinary citizens. The result is a contradiction at the heart of contemporary democratic capitalism. Political systems proclaim the sovereignty of the people while economic institutions frequently organize social life according to imperatives that remain beyond meaningful democratic control. The Work of Democratic Renewal Defending American democracy requires a broad commitment to institutional accountability, civic participation, and the restoration of public trust. Independent courts, a free press, fair elections, and meaningful legislative oversight remain essential. Political leaders must be held accountable when they violate the law or attempt to undermine the constitutional responsibilities of their offices. But institutional defense alone is insufficient. Democracy also requires citizens capable of distinguishing evidence from propaganda, recognizing the historical origins of political conflict, and participating in collective deliberation without surrendering their judgment to charismatic leaders. Education consequently occupies a central position in any serious project of democratic renewal. Related: The Pedagogy of the Heart: Music, Memory, and the Pursuit of Social Justice The Republic Is Not Yet Its Future The American republic stands at a dangerous historical juncture, but its future is not predetermined. Authoritarian movements draw strength from real contradictions, unresolved injustices, and widespread disillusionment. They flourish when democratic institutions appear incapable of addressing ordinary people's needs and when political discourse becomes dominated by resentment, fear, and the search for enemies. To resist these movements effectively, democratic forces must do more than condemn their rhetoric. They must confront the conditions that make authoritarian promises attractive. They must demonstrate that democratic government can address economic insecurity, protect individual rights, strengthen public institutions, and expand opportunities for meaningful participation. They must recover the conviction that political freedom and social justice are not opposing objectives but mutually reinforcing dimensions of a genuinely democratic society. The task also requires historical honesty. American democracy has never been a completed achievement. Its history includes slavery, dispossession, exclusion, imperial ambition, and the concentration of economic power. Yet it also includes generations of people who challenged those injustices and struggled to enlarge the meaning of freedom. The democratic tradition is therefore neither an immaculate inheritance nor an irredeemable failure. It is an unfinished historical struggle whose direction depends upon the actions of those who inherit it. We must resist the temptation to regard democracy as something guaranteed by the mere survival of familiar institutions. Constitutions cannot defend themselves. Courts cannot preserve their independence without public support. Elections cannot sustain democratic legitimacy when political leaders systematically undermine the conditions of fair competition. Citizens cannot exercise meaningful freedom if they are deprived of the knowledge, resources, and collective agency necessary to participate in public life. Democracy must be continually renewed through practice. The struggle for American democracy is consequently part of a larger struggle over the future of humanity. Across the world, societies confront the concentration of wealth, ecological devastation, political polarization, technological transformation, and the growing capacity of powerful institutions to shape human life without meaningful public accountability. These challenges demand more than nostalgia for an earlier political order. They require the courage to imagine democratic possibilities that existing institutions have yet to realize. The future of the republic will depend upon whether Americans can recover the distinction between power and legitimacy, between national greatness and national domination, between political loyalty and democratic responsibility. It will depend upon whether citizens can recognize that the freedom of others is not a threat to their own, that criticism is not treason, and that the capacity to question authority is among the most important safeguards of a free society. It will depend, finally, upon whether democracy can become more than a system for selecting leaders and recover its deeper meaning as a collective commitment to human dignity, social justice, and the unfinished possibilities of historical transformation. The republic is not simply what its founders imagined, nor is it merely what its current leaders proclaim it to be. It is what successive generations make of it through their struggles, their failures, their solidarities, and their willingness to confront the contradictions of their own time. No political leader can guarantee its future. No constitution can substitute for the active participation of citizens. No appeal to national greatness can compensate for the abandonment of democratic responsibility. The struggle continues because the promise remains unfinished. The future remains unwritten. But it will not be written for us.

articles.title: The 1956 Hungarian Uprising Was a Working-Class Revolt
articles.author: Adam Fabry
articles.content: On October 23, 1956, tens of thousands of Hungarians took to the streets of Budapest. What began as a demonstration led largely by students rapidly became a popular uprising against the country’s Stalinist government. Within days, the authority of the Hungarian Communist Party had crumbled, Soviet troops had been forced to withdraw, and workers across the country were establishing their own councils to organize production and exercise political power. The Soviet leadership called it a “counterrevolution,” while Western governments celebrated it as a “revolt against communism.” Both interpretations obscured something fundamental: the Hungarian Revolution was driven by workers and ordinary people who wanted to free themselves from a system that claimed to represent their interests. The uprising was ultimately crushed by Soviet military intervention on November 4. Thousands were killed; hundreds were executed in the repression that followed; and some two hundred thousand Hungarians fled the country. Yet the revolution remains one of the twentieth century’s most important challenges to authoritarian rule in the name of socialism. For the international Left, its significance is difficult to overstate. As the Hungarian Marxist philosopher G. M. Tamás observed, Eastern Europe was precisely where socialism had supposedly been put into practice. What, then, were we to make of workers rising en masse against a self-proclaimed socialist government? The answer begins with the contradictions of the Hungarian state itself — and with the people who dared to challenge it. The Crisis of Stalinist Hungary By the mid-1950s, Hungary was a country of roughly ten million people still recovering from the devastation of World War II. Following the defeat of Nazi Germany, it had been incorporated into the Soviet sphere of influence. Its economy was reorganized around state ownership, central planning, and rapid industrialization, while political power was concentrated in the hands of a Communist Party modeled on the ruling party in Joseph Stalin’s Soviet Union. Under the leadership of Mátyás Rákosi, the party pursued an especially brutal version of this model. Heavy industry received priority over consumer goods, agriculture was subjected to forced collectivization, and living standards were sacrificed to ambitious production targets. The secret police, known as the State Protection Authority (ÁVH), became the instrument of a pervasive system of surveillance, intimidation, and repression. The government justified these policies on the grounds that they were necessary for building socialism. But workers had little control over their workplaces, peasants faced coercive agricultural policies, and ordinary citizens had virtually no say in political decisions. Although the state owned the factories, that did not mean power was in the hands of the people who worked in those factories. From a critical political-economic perspective, this exposed a deeper contradiction. The state mobilized society for rapid industrial accumulation while subordinating workers to the demands of production. The bureaucracy determined what was produced, how resources were allocated, and how much people were expected to sacrifice. The facade was socialist, but the relationship between rulers and ruled remained profoundly authoritarian. The New Course The unexpected death of Stalin in 1953 opened a small space for change. Under pressure from Moscow, Rákosi was replaced as prime minister by Imre Nagy, a reform-minded Communist who recognized that the existing economic model was unsustainable. The new government introduced economic and political reforms, known as the “New Course,” which promised to reduce the emphasis on heavy industry, improve living standards, expand consumer production, and ease political repression. The reforms generated widespread hopes. Forced labor camps were closed, restrictions on private enterprise were relaxed, and peasants received greater freedom to cultivate their land. But the success of the reform program was far from guaranteed. Rákosi retained control of the party apparatus, and powerful Stalinist factions opposed Nagy’s attempts to change course. In 1955, with Soviet support, Nagy’s opponents accused him of “right-wing deviation” and had him removed from office. His dismissal signaled that the state would not tolerate even limited reform when it threatened the authority of the party bureaucracy. The following year, Nikita Khrushchev’s denunciation of Stalin’s crimes at the Soviet Communist Party’s Twentieth Congress further undermined the regime’s legitimacy. If Moscow now acknowledged the terror and injustice of Stalin’s rule, what did that mean for the Hungarian leaders who had faithfully reproduced his methods? Students, intellectuals, writers, and increasingly workers began demanding answers. By October 1956, Hungary was like a tinderbox waiting to explode. A Revolution Takes Shape The immediate spark came on October 23. Students gathered in Budapest to demand political reform, the return of Imre Nagy to government, the withdrawal of Soviet troops, and greater national independence. Their demands also encompassed changes to workplace conditions, including opposition to the unpopular piece-rate system that tied workers’ wages to production quotas. The demonstration grew dramatically as people joined the march through the capital. By evening, a vast crowd had assembled outside parliament. Elsewhere, demonstrators pulled down a monumental statue of Stalin, an unmistakable declaration that the old order had lost its authority. The plinth upon which a large statue of Stalin had stood before October 23, 1956. Only the Stalin figure’s boots remain. (Pesti srác2 / CC BY-SA 3.0 ) The turning point came when demonstrators gathered outside the Hungarian Radio headquarters, hoping to broadcast their demands. ÁVH security forces opened fire, killing and wounding people. The violent response by the government transformed a mass demonstration into an armed uprising. Weapons were seized, police vehicles were set ablaze, and insurgents began confronting the state’s armed forces. The head of a Stalin statue sits in the middle of a Budapest street, on October 23, 1956. (Hofbauer Róbert / CC BY-SA 3.0 ) The following day, Soviet troops entered Budapest, but their intervention failed to restore order. Some Hungarian soldiers refused to fight the insurgents; others defected or handed over weapons. Nagy returned to the premiership as the authorities struggled to regain control. What had begun as a protest against political repression was becoming something much more radical. The uprising spread beyond the capital to industrial towns, provincial centers, and rural communities. Factories stopped working, local revolutionary committees appeared, and workers began organizing independently of the party and the state. Workers’ Councils This is where the conventional Cold War story becomes inadequate. The revolution cannot be understood simply as a national revolt against Soviet occupation, nor as an uprising orchestrated by anti-communist politicians. Its most consequential development was the emergence of independent working-class organization. Across Hungary, workers established revolutionary councils, elected by their colleagues and answerable to them. These bodies coordinated strikes, organized supplies, represented workers in negotiations, and increasingly asserted authority over factories and local institutions. They were not merely trade unions demanding higher wages. In many cases, they challenged the state’s right to govern workplaces and society without popular consent. Historical estimates suggest that more than two thousand workers’ councils were established during the revolution, involving more than 28,000 members. Their demands varied, but recurring themes included the withdrawal of Soviet troops, political freedoms, the release of prisoners, and genuine worker participation in economic decision-making. For a brief moment, the factory floor became a site of political power. Workers who had supposedly constituted the ruling class discovered that they could organize production and articulate political demands without the supervision of party officials. The revolution was not ideologically uniform. It brought together students, industrial workers, peasants, intellectuals, reform Communists, and supporters of different political traditions. Nor did all its participants share the same vision of Hungary’s future. But the workers’ councils gave the uprising a distinctive social character that neither the Soviet leadership nor its Western adversaries could comfortably accommodate. Beyond Budapest The working-class dimension of the revolution was particularly evident in Budapest’s industrial districts and in provincial manufacturing centers. Workers in Csepel, Újpest, and Kőbánya joined the resistance, while industrial towns such as Miskolc, Ózd, and Dunapentele (which had been renamed Sztálinváros under the Stalinist regime) became important sites of revolutionary activity. These developments matter because the revolution is often remembered primarily through images of street fighting in Budapest. Yet the uprising spread through the networks of industrial production, workplaces, and communities that underpinned the Hungarian economy. In Dunapentele, workers insisted that their town was socialist precisely because its inhabitants were workers and power belonged in their hands. They declared their intention to defend it against both fascist excesses and Soviet troops. Their statement captured the central contradiction of 1956: they were not necessarily rejecting the ideal of socialism but rejecting a political order that invoked socialism to justify its own domination. Peter Fryer was a correspondent for the Daily Worker , the official newspaper of the Communist Party of Great Britain. He witnessed the uprising and described the devastation inflicted on Budapest by Soviet forces. Working-class districts suffered particularly heavily. Fryer’s reports challenged the official Communist account of a fascist conspiracy and helped expose the reality of the intervention to readers abroad. Workers’ participation was not limited to the construction of councils or the organization of strikes. They also formed a substantial part of the armed resistance. Fighting was particularly intense in industrial neighborhoods, where insurgents used their knowledge of local streets and buildings to resist a much-better-equipped military force. Young workers were especially prominent. Many had grown up under the Communist regime, experienced its workplace discipline and political restrictions, and reached adulthood with little memory of the prewar order. The motivation behind their revolt cannot be reduced to nostalgia for the old Hungary. They were challenging the society in which they had actually lived. The distinction is crucial. The revolution did contain nationalist and anti-communist currents, and some participants sought a restoration of political arrangements from before the war. But these currents do not explain the independent organization of workers across the country, nor do they justify the Soviet claim that military intervention was necessary to defeat a fascist counterrevolution. The revolution’s social diversity should not obscure its central achievement: ordinary people began to exercise political power for themselves. The Soviet Counterattack By late October, the uprising had forced the government into a series of concessions. Nagy announced a coalition government and, under mounting pressure, moved toward political pluralism. On October 28, the government declared a ceasefire and acknowledged the revolutionary movement. The prospect of Soviet withdrawal appeared increasingly real. But the Soviet leadership faced a dilemma. Allowing Hungary to break decisively from Moscow’s control risked destabilizing the entire Soviet bloc. The danger was not merely that another government might leave the Warsaw Pact. It was that a successful revolution organized from below might inspire workers elsewhere to challenge their own rulers. The crisis also unfolded against a wider international backdrop. Western powers were unwilling to risk a direct military confrontation with the Soviet Union, while the Suez crisis was exposing the limits of Western claims to defend freedom and national sovereignty. Hungary’s fate would ultimately be decided by the balance of power between states, not by the rhetoric of either superpower. On November 1, Nagy announced Hungary’s withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact and appealed for international recognition of the country’s neutrality. Meanwhile, Moscow had already begun preparing a second military intervention. In the early hours of November 4, Soviet forces launched Operation Whirlwind, attacking Budapest and other centers of resistance. This time the assault was overwhelming. Some 58,000 Soviet troops advanced against a revolution that lacked the military resources to withstand a prolonged offensive. Hungarian army units were rapidly disarmed or neutralized, while workers and insurgents continued fighting in several areas. Nagy broadcasted a desperate appeal for help announcing that Soviet forces had attacked the capital and were attempting to overthrow the government. He subsequently sought refuge in the Yugoslav embassy, but was later arrested. In 1958, following a secret trial, he was executed alongside other leaders of the revolution, including Pál Maléter. By November 11, the main centers of armed resistance had been crushed. More than 2,500 people had died during the revolution. The workers’ councils, however, did not immediately disappear. Their continued existence forced the new authorities to confront a problem that military victory alone could not resolve: how to govern a population that had demonstrated such open hostility to the regime. Defeat and the Consolidation of Kádár’s Rule While Soviet tanks were reentering Hungary, a new Soviet-friendly government, led by János Kádár, was formed. However, the new government initially faced widespread opposition. Factories remained closed, transport services were disrupted, and workers organized strikes against the Soviet intervention. The Central Workers’ Council of Greater Budapest, established in November, became a focal point for efforts to coordinate resistance and negotiate with the authorities. The government responded with a mixture of concessions and repression. Kádár’s representatives negotiated with workers’ leaders, seeking to persuade them to resume production. But when negotiations failed to break the resistance, the authorities turned decisively toward coercion. On December 9, the headquarters of the Central Workers’ Council was raided and prominent activists were arrested. Martial law was imposed, strikes were criminalized, and imprisonment and execution became instruments of political control. By early 1957, organized resistance was increasingly difficult to sustain. Many young workers fled Hungary, while those who remained faced the prospect of prison, dismissal, or forced submission. The repression was followed by a longer process of political consolidation. Kádár rebuilt the Communist Party (now renamed the Hungarian Socialist Workers’ Party, MSZMP) and sought to win the acquiescence of a population exhausted by conflict. Over time, his government developed a more pragmatic approach to economic management and everyday life. Compared with the brutalities of the Rákosi period, Kádár’s Hungary eventually became associated with relative material security and a degree of private autonomy. But these accommodations rested on the defeat of independent political organization. Workers could enjoy certain improvements in living standards, provided they did not seek to reclaim the political power they had briefly exercised in 1956. The revolution therefore left a complicated legacy. Its defeat did not mean that Hungarian society returned unchanged to the prerevolutionary order. The authorities had learned that permanent mobilization, relentless austerity, and indiscriminate terror could undermine the stability they sought to secure. The memory of 1956 placed limits on the state’s room for maneuver, even as it tried to erase the revolution’s independent working-class character. The Legacy of 1956 Today The struggle over the meaning of 1956 did not end with the defeat of the revolution. In contemporary Hungary, its memory remains contested. Following the democratic transition in 1989–90, political commemorations have often emphasized themes of national independence and resistance to Soviet domination that primarily resonate with the emphasis of right-wing political parties on national sovereignty. Under Viktor Orbán’s sixteen-year rule, the state invested heavily in creating an institutionally revisionist memory culture in Hungary, presenting the revolution as a reactionary struggle for “national sovereignty.” However, this picture is utterly detached from the reality of what was happening on the ground in 1956. While reactionary forces sought to co-opt the revolutionary movement at the time, as often happens in mass politics, the struggle did not lose its principled socialist character. The interpretation that stresses the issue of national sovereignty obscures the revolution’s equally important challenge to domestic authoritarianism and the power of political elites. The workers’ councils should remind us that we cannot separate opposition to foreign domination from the question of who exercises power within society. The revolution was not simply a nation asserting its independence; it was also a population challenging a ruling class that claimed to represent it. The lesson extends well beyond Hungary. At a time when authoritarian movements are gaining ground across Europe and elsewhere, 1956 challenges the assumption that political alternatives must be confined to a choice between authoritarian state control and the existing capitalist order. It also offers a warning to the Left: governments cannot claim to represent working people while denying them the freedom to organize independently, challenge political authority, and determine the conditions under which they live and work. The legacy of 1956 is therefore neither simply nationalist nor merely anti-communist. It is a reminder that emancipation cannot be imposed from above, whether in the name of socialism, national security, or economic progress. The Hungarian workers who challenged their rulers demonstrated that democracy means more than choosing between competing elites. It also means the collective capacity of ordinary people to shape their own lives. This crucial class aspect is often excluded from today’s discourse: many commentators attempt to draw parallels with the war in Ukraine, which often reduces this pivotal socialist revolution to merely a struggle for national sovereignty. What 1956 Means for the Left The Hungarian Revolution was neither a vindication of liberal capitalism nor the reactionary conspiracy portrayed by Soviet propaganda. It was a heterogeneous popular uprising whose most radical expression lay in the independent organization of workers. That distinction remains politically important. If socialism means only state ownership, central planning, and rule by a party claiming exclusive authority to represent the working class, then the Hungarian workers’ revolt poses an uncomfortable question: What happens when the people supposedly represented by the state rise up against it? We cannot find the answer by dismissing the revolution as an aberration or by ignoring the political diversity of its participants. It requires taking seriously the experience of workers who challenged bureaucratic control, organized their workplaces, and demanded the right to determine their own future. The councils did not offer a complete blueprint for a socialist society. They operated under extraordinary circumstances, and their political projects were neither uniform nor free of contradictions. But they demonstrated that opposition to Stalinism could emerge from a desire for greater democracy and collective control, rather than simply a wish to restore capitalism. For the Left, the lesson is not that the revolution should be claimed uncritically by any particular tradition. It is that socialism cannot be reduced to the power of the state, and workers cannot be treated as passive beneficiaries of policies devised in their name. Emancipation requires their active participation in shaping economic and political life. In 1956, Hungarian workers confronted a regime that claimed to have abolished exploitation while denying them meaningful control over their labor and society. Their defeat exposed the violence required to preserve that contradiction. It also revealed the possibility of another kind of politics — one rooted in collective self-organization, political freedom, and the struggle against domination. The Soviet tanks crushed the revolution. They could not entirely extinguish its challenge to the meaning of socialism. For anyone on the Left still committed to a society governed democratically by those who create its wealth, that challenge remains unfinished. articles.title: Blue Wave Is Here
articles.author: William J. Astore
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I woke to the news of a “blue wave” as Democrats regained control of the House and Senate by margins that few predicted. It was a resounding rebuke to the Trump and MAGA crowd, which can’t be a bad thing. But it isn’t a moment where, as the saying goes, we can all go back to brunch and let a Democrat-controlled Congress handle things. We have to stay involved, for the mess in Washington is very much a bipartisan one. The “new” House and Senate majority leaders will be Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, corporate Democrats who support Zionist Israel and gleefully accept money and marching orders from AIPAC. That is unlikely to change much, as the power exercised by these men isn’t easy to challenge since they control the money and the perks for their party. Still, there are more populists/progressives elected this time around, so perhaps Hakeem and Chuck will discover new masks to don. These are men who are flexible like Gumby when it comes to principles, so it’s up to the newly elected Members of Congress, as well as people like us, to demand real change rather than the cosmetic version they’re most comfortable at selling. Related: Trump's One-Man Horror Show Continues Americans are most certainly tired of war; will Democrats finally act to end Trump’s unconstitutional and disastrous war against Iran? What about support of Zionist Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza? Will Democrats finally stop all the U.S. military equipment flowing to Israel even if it hurts American manufacturers of the same? Trump, of course, has already promised to veto anything a Democratic-led Congress tries to do for a saner and safer world. I saw today that Trump says he will accept the election results, as the New York Times put it. How generous and gracious of him! It’s like accepting that the sun came up this morning. If Trump really does veto everything, a friend suggested that Democrats should force him to “veto a wealth tax for billionaires, veto a pause on data center construction, veto a restoration of healthcare to millions, veto a cut off of military aid to Israel and other authoritarian regimes, etc. This would set up [Democrats] for a 2028 victory.” That’s a sensible strategy, but whether Democrats have the discipline and commitment to follow it is questionable. Related: When Everything Is Political, What Happens to Art? Still, as another friend put it this morning, let’s enjoy the rebuke of Trump and MAGA before Democrats start gathering their usual circular firing squad. Seriously, yesterday’s election sent a clear message that Americans are fed up and want a government that actually serves them rather than the usual suspects at the top. Now, we have to push our new “leaders” to govern in that spirit. It’s not time to go back to brunch. It’s time to keep pushing politicians to serve the public rather than the plutocrats and the powerful. Readers, what did you take from the election results? Are you more hopeful today? Remember, however, that “hope is not a plan.”

articles.title: OPINION: Understanding 2026 State Ballot Questions in Massachusetts
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: By: Central Mass & Worcester DSA The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not represent the official position of Working Mass. Our goal in putting out this explainer is not mainly to convince you to vote one way or another. In fact, this explainer is not targeted only at voters. We want all working-class people to understand what a circus so much of this is and also where our real power lies. You’ll notice not all nine of this year’s ballot questions are here. Again, we don’t aim to offer a comprehensive set of voting instructions to guide you through voting for each question. This is not a voter guide. Instead, we hope this explainer will illuminate causes, solutions, and forces at play, and we see the ballot questions that we’ve selected as being well-suited to that purpose. That doesn’t mean there aren’t questions where we have a clear stance — for example, on Question 2 to extend union rights to public defenders, we support worker organizing, regardless of any law. Our support, however, does not extend to police, an arm of the state that represses workers, and we challenge the legitimacy of the capitalist criminal-legal system. Our socialist perspective, on these questions and so much more, is distinct from that of liberals, and we want to expose misdirection and deception by capitalist parties and the ways that laws and the state serve particular economic interests. With this explainer, we seek to go beyond the narrow framing of these questions and raise far bigger ones about our capitalist society. Join us! How we think about elections We’re socialists, and our aim is socialism, which means, in the plainest terms, a seizure of political power by the working class, a democratic socialization of ownership of our economy, and an economic system in which our labor power is no longer a commodity. As said in our Principles for Socialist Electoral Work , we see U.S. elections, and those in any capitalist democracy, as largely a sham. They mislead people into thinking our hand is on the wheel when really they decide which faction of the ruling class will take it for the next few years. Even without the Electoral College, Senate, gerrymandering, and judicial review, the system is thoroughly undemocratic. The equality of participants is superficial and purely legal because the intense concentration of wealth and economic power inherent to capitalism inevitably translates into a tremendous concentration and inequality of political power, incompatible with democracy. And we refer not only to campaign spending, lobbying, and the media, but to private ownership of the means of production by the capitalist class and their devastating power — no matter who is elected — to withdraw investment as they please, throttling the economy and all of us with it. So, we’re clear-eyed about the nature of elections, and yet, still we participate. Socialists must champion struggles for reforms, not because reforms offer a way out of capitalism — they don’t — but to raise class consciousness and build a socialist party, which do. Electoral work offers opportunities not for fleeting policy or election wins but subordinate to higher, political aims: reaching and organizing the masses, dispelling illusions, and broadcasting our socialist politics. What are these questions on my ballot? Ballot questions in Massachusetts can seek to pass or repeal a law and are also required for constitutional amendments. Interest groups use them when they want to change the state constitution or cannot get the state legislature to fund, act on, or stay away from their priorities. For example, Question 6 seeks to reserve some existing sales tax revenue for conservation and is driven by conservation groups that want to force the legislature to redirect state funding to their priority. Question 8 was initiated by a Virginia-based anti-marijuana group now spending millions to try to end Massachusetts’s multibillion-dollar recreational marijuana industry. Similarly, Question 9 is driven by gun owners wanting to roll back state regulations on gun ownership to what they were before October 2024, when the governor signed a new gun law. Because state laws typically require tens of thousands of signatures to put questions on the statewide ballot and because these campaigns can sometimes necessitate millions in spending to win, statewide ballot question campaigns typically need to be well-funded. Naturally, that means many ballot questions end up being initiated by capital against the interests of labor. It should be noted too that the state legislature can stop constitutional amendments from even making it to the ballot and has the power to change or undo laws passed by ballot question. Likewise, the courts can throw out questions as well. You might know, for example, that the state legislature has battled against implementing a ballot question passed in 2024 authorizing the state auditor to audit the legislature, and that the state Supreme Court stopped rent control from appearing on your ballot this year. They have constitutional objections — our critiques are on the actual merits — but our stance is not one of demanding binding legislation by ballot question. That’s because the root cause of this crisis of democracy is the structure of the legislature itself and the classes that it represents. In a socialist world, with the working class exercising truly democratic control in their workplaces and over all of society, we could have a proportionally elected body recallable by workers, and ballot questions to circumvent a legislature wouldn’t be necessary at all. In fact, the supremacy of a legislature could be an asset to and an instrument of a working class that wielded it. But in the meantime, we know that power is not expressed by passing ballot questions. No, the power of our class comes from its indispensable role in production. “Without our brain and muscle” — without our labor — “not a single wheel can turn.” There are many things the state legislature will never willingly allow, but organized mass action can compel it. If the choice is between radical changes and the economy grinding to a halt, radical changes will indeed come. A major task for the socialist movement is to build up to that moment and then to go further still and dispense with the capitalist state and its state legislatures altogether, instituting a workers republic and putting the working class in charge of its destiny. In Central Mass & Worcester DSA, all of our efforts in the electoral arena are toward this end and for that day. The Central Mass & Worcester DSA membership democratically approved this ballot question explainer in lieu of a traditional voter guide. articles.title: Mandate Is Affordability
articles.author: Unai Montes-Irueste
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Before we’re buried in hot takes on what the midterms mean, here is what we know: no one can afford anything. The mandate of this election is that costs have to come down and wages have to go up. Voters told pollsters that the cost of living and government corruption weighed heavily on them , and they voted accordingly. Democrats won, and in historic fashion. The party is projected to hold at least 54 Senate seats after flipping seven Republican-held seats , and NBC News estimates Democrats will hold at least 258 House seats, the widest House margin in 33 years. Counts are still being finalized. The GOP could lose even more. But the Democratic Party writ large still has a net negative favorability rating (and for good reason). Voters did not hand Democrats a blank check. They handed this new legislative majority a mandate with a deadline. Related: Who Is Buying the 26th State Senate Seat? Who delivered the win The coalition that delivered victory in 2020 but unraveled in 2024 has returned. In the NBC News exit poll , voters ages 18 to 29 backed Democratic House candidates 72–25, Black voters 89–9, Latino voters 62–35, and Asian American voters 70–29. Tufts’ CIRCLE found Black (90%), Asian (84%), and Latino (78%) youth gave Democrats the strongest support, and AP’s VoteCast shows young and Latino voters moving away from Republicans in contrast to what we saw in 2024. In Texas, where Democrats had not won statewide in more than 30 years , James Talarico was projected to win the Senate race . Jewish voters were the exception. The NBC exit poll found half now identify as Democrats, down from 64% in 2018 , though a Jewish Electorate Institute survey still showed a 71–23 Democratic edge on the congressional ballot. In Michigan, Muslim voters backed Abdul El-Sayed 92–8 in the same exit poll. Solid data on Native American voters is scarce , though dedicated 2022 polling found Native voters leaning Democratic. Exit polls are estimates, not final counts. But there is no indication that anyone other than white men and white women decided to stick with GOP candidates for federal office. There are no pure market solutions I have already seen too many people with big platforms warn that the DSA wing of the party will lead to ruin and a lost White House in 2028. What they miss is that there are no pure market solutions to the mess we are in. American history is clear: the only way to undo inequality is to break up concentrated corporate power. Congress passed the Sherman Act in 1890, and it sat mostly idle until Theodore Roosevelt’s administration sued to break up Northern Securities , a railroad trust backed by J.P. Morgan and John D. Rockefeller. The Supreme Court ruled against the trust 5–4 in 1904 , and in 1911 it ordered Standard Oil dissolved into 34 companies. Roosevelt sued 45 companies and Taft sued 75 . The robber barons did not volunteer. Today’s answer is the same: anti-trust, anti-monopoly, anti-robber-baron action, embraced without hedging or moderation. Workers need the same muscle. There is no security in employment in the AI era unless it is locked in by a collective bargaining agreement, which means a rapid expansion of labor unions. And the 2028 Democratic nominee will almost certainly run on taxing billionaire wealth and closing the loopholes that let companies like Amazon pay $0 in federal income tax in years of record profit. Related: AI Isn’t the Industrial Revolution. It’s the Ice Age. The gorillas in the room Let me be clear about my expectations. I fully expect that the fight over U.S. policy toward Israel will be ongoing. The October 27 Politico/Morning Consult Poll highlighted growing American indifference and negative sentiment toward Israeli leadership. 48 percent of U.S. adults viewed Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as either entirely unjustified or initially justified but having gone too far. According to tracking data from the Yale Youth Poll , roughly two-thirds of voters under 30 support reducing or entirely ending U.S. military aid to Israel. This isn't just a progressive trend; a June 2026 Anadolu Agency report highlighted that 51% of Republican voters under 45 would prefer a 2028 presidential primary candidate who supports reducing weapons shipments. Because the existing U.S.-Israel aid agreement runs through 2028 and funding remains subject to congressional appropriations, the new Democratic-led Congress could wield substantial influence over how this issue unfolds. Legislation will be debated but I am positive that Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer will do everything in their power to avoid a showdown. (Expect it to be a 2028 litmus test). Similarly, I do not expect Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer to propose solutions at the scale of the housing crisis. But once Democrats have gone after tariffs, gasoline, grocery prices, electricity and water bills, and the data center boom, housing is the elephant, the gorilla, and whatever other proverbial animal remains in the room. It cannot be handled by tinkering around the edges. Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies reports a record 22.7 million cost-burdened renter households , including 12.1 million paying more than half their income on housing, and a 7.2 million-unit shortage of homes affordable and available to extremely low-income renters. No “tax credit” or “opportunity zone” closes a gap that size. We need a national rent control policy, government-built housing for rent and sale, and real protection from eviction and displacement. Otherwise we keep playing fast and loose with meaningless statistics while the American Dream slips out of reach for half the country. Climate makes it worse. More hurricanes, tornadoes, and wildfires will destroy homes every year. A chronically underfunded FEMA, and an insurance and disaster recovery market that punishes working-class and middle-class families, are symptoms of a bigger problem. The put-up-or-shut-up budget The worst provisions of Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) arrive with the new year. Medicaid work requirements take effect January 1, 2027 , with the SNAP and hospital closure crisis close behind. The nonpartisan CBO projects that the OBBBA will increase the number of uninsured Americans by 10 million by 2034. When factoring in the baseline expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits, organizations like the Center for American Progress estimate total coverage losses could reach 16 million people. Studies mapping insurance loss to public health outcomes yield widely different conclusions, ranging from 1,500 to 51,000 preventable deaths annually. Democrats will have to play hardball in annual budget negotiations, send bills that may be vetoed, and then find enough Republicans to override. Healthcare, ending the Iran war, and fully funding FEMA may be the only places Republican support is within reach. The White House and the Pentagon are aggressively seeking a war funding package from Congress. The administration has requested an emergency supplemental blueprint of $70 billion to retroactively cover unfunded 2026 operations and secure short-term future funding. Taking money from the Iran war, and taking it from ICE, whose budget got a $75 billion infusion from OBBBA, is the play. Related: Southern California Edison Is a Predatory Corporation Getting Rich Off a Basic Human Need ICE is not a bodycam problem The leadership has already had a chance on ICE. After the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis , Democrats blocked DHS funding over a list of demands: body cameras, masks off, and judicial warrants . Republicans said they were open to body cameras , which a bill already funded, and the standoff dragged through repeated failed Senate votes while ICE kept running on its reconciliation money. A separate Democratic push in the House to mandate body cameras failed in committee . Oversight, training, and cameras are not what Latino voters came out for. We are furious at what ICE has done. Folks want ICE out of our communities and stripped of its budget, and they want the people who killed, maimed, and tore families apart fired, prosecuted, and jailed. Several Democrats, such as Sen. John Fetterman and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, are lousy on immigration, so Democrats will need to act while fighting their own. Clean house Democratic leaders must also pass ethics rules, even over a veto, that bar anyone in federal elected or appointed office from using it for personal enrichment: no stock trades, blind trusts for all investments, no gifts from foreign powers. The record shows why. Oil futures worth more than $500 million traded in the 15 minutes before Trump’s March 23 announcement pausing strikes on Iran, prompting Rep. Ritchie Torres to ask the SEC and CFTC to investigate. Trades before the April 2025 tariff pause and a Polymarket trader’s roughly $400,000 bet on Maduro’s capture also drew suspicion, and a soldier was arrested over alleged Maduro bets . Trump’s disclosure reportedly shows he bought 327 stocks the day before the tariff pause . The White House warned staff not to bet on the war. None of these allegations has been proven, which is the point of an investigation. Even Republican James Comer has expanded a House probe into prediction markets. This is not only a Trump problem. Bipartisan efforts to restrict congressional stock trades have stalled , and the Supreme Court, where gifts from billionaire Harlan Crow to Justice Clarence Thomas drew scrutiny, adopted a code of conduct with no enforcement mechanism . Court packing, term limits, or impeachment may be unlikely, but ethics standards applied across the federal government are achievable. Democrats can and should make this literally criminal. The story we owe each other 2028 will be the first $1 trillion election. Beyond the candidate spending, AI, crypto, and other corporations will break records. Billionaires will pour unprecedented dollars into pop-up PACs. None of these bad actors will win over voters with straightforward arguments. They will lie. How do we know? Because they just showed us their hand in races across the country where they defeated candidates who sought to regulate them by painting corporate candidates as progressives, and progressive candidates as hypocrites. The issue of inequality is so egregious that it isn't going anywhere anytime soon. Everyone wants to see something done about it, but not everyone agrees on what to do. There is a lesson here. In 2020 the Movement for Black Lives drove change while the country was polarized over COVID, with no agreement on what to do. Many who rejected science and vaccines went on to form the MAHA movement around RFK Jr., which helped deliver the White House to Trump in 2024. We could head into 2028 the same way: a lot of people angry about inequality, but little agreement on what to do beyond stopping data center sprawl. In 2020 there was a willingness to confront a broken criminal justice system. In 2028 we need the same willingness to confront a broken immigration system. Without that engine, we will be stuck in a contest of personalities (and egos). A government of the people, by the people, and for the people shall not perish, But a people without a vision shall. We need a story for We the People for the next generation. Let us begin writing it now.

articles.title: We Need a Socialist Congressional Caucus
articles.author: Nick French
articles.content: With last night’s election results , it’s official: after new members are sworn in this coming January, socialists will hold more seats in Congress than they ever have in US history. Six freshmen congress members backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) — Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Chris Rabb of Philadelphia, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, and Angela Gonzales-Torres of Los Angeles — are joining fellow DSA members Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib in the House of Representatives. Counting also Sen. Bernie Sanders, long a self-described democratic socialist though not officially affiliated with DSA, the United States will have nine socialist members of Congress. The new socialist legislators, all of whom ran on the Democratic Party ballot line, can be expected (like Tlaib, AOC, and Sanders) to caucus with the Democrats. Despite achieving a meaningful beachhead in the legislature and being joined by left-populist allies like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Maine’s Troy Jackson, socialists will still be a tiny minority within the Democratic caucus. The growing left wing will have to figure out how to coordinate effectively with each other while operating within the “big tent” of the larger congressional party. That party is full of members committed to pro-corporate and militarist agendas, and avowed anti-socialists Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer are likely to be its leaders. The socialist legislators, on the other hand, have their own policy priorities and were elected in large part because of their criticisms of the party establishment: for failing to address the cost-of-living crisis, for backing Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and for mounting an ineffective opposition to Donald Trump’s attacks on workers and civil rights. To navigate the terrain of Congress effectively, including the inevitable conflicts with corporate-friendly Democrats and party leaders, socialists need their own congressional caucus. The Need for a Socialist Caucus Members of Congress on both sides of the aisle have long recognized the utility of cooperating with ideologically like-minded legislators in smaller caucuses within the larger legislative parties. The Democrats’ three main ideological caucuses are the Blue Dogs, representing the right wing of the party; the New Democrat Coalition (NDC), representing a basically socially liberal but economically moderate faction; and the Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC), representing the party’s left-leaning members. These caucuses are venues for legislators to formulate ideas and coordinate strategy. They can serve to advance particular priorities that don’t have the support of the broader party, or at least not yet. They also signal members’ broad alignment with distinct ideological currents within the broad Democratic tent. Sanders, Tlaib, and AOC are already members of the CPC, and Sanders himself helped found the caucus (along with late DSA member Ron Dellums and others) in 1991. So it may seem like the new socialist electeds are better off simply joining the CPC and attempting to advance their priorities that way. Yet that caucus long ago ceased to be an ideologically cohesive organization, let alone one that can be expected to fight for socialist legislative goals. As Jacobin contributor Neal Meyer has written , many CPC members have refused to back left-wing priorities like Medicare for All or reducing our country’s obscene military budget. And today, many CPC members are also members of the centrist, pro-business NDC. In fact, the incumbents ousted by DSA challengers this cycle — Adriano Espaillat, Diana DeGette, Shri Thanedar, and Jimmy Gomez — were members of the CPC. What a Caucus Can Achieve So there’s a real role to be played by a new caucus that can cohere left-wing elected officials and continue efforts to build a socialist pole within the Democratic Party, expanding on the work that politicians like Sanders, AOC, and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani have done already. In the short term, a socialist caucus may be able to make strategic interventions to advance its policy aims (and block bad policy). Here they might learn a thing or two from the House Freedom Caucus (HFC), the hard-right GOP caucus founded in 2015 that was instrumental in ousting House Speaker Kevin McCarthy and replacing him with Mike Johnson. The Freedom Caucus has often played “ legislative hardball ” against its own party to try to push policy further right. Looking at the HFC experience, scholar of the GOP Paul Heideman writes , “The conditions in which socialist legislative hardball is most likely to be successful are those in which the Democratic Party has a majority in Congress and an opposite-party president.” That is the situation in which socialists will soon find themselves. In similar circumstances, the HFC was able to “use its size and discipline to compel the House leadership to enter into fights with the administration that it otherwise would have avoided” and “succeeded in winning more power for itself in the form of committee appointments and so on.” The very large congressional majority that Democrats just won , however, means that socialists will not be able to constitute a winning vote margin, which puts limits on their leverage. Heideman has also observed that the hardball strategy has often been counterproductive. Sometimes, when Freedom Caucus members refused to vote for legislation because it was insufficiently right-wing, Republican leadership was forced to seek Democratic votes to pass the legislation instead. As a result, the legislation ended up more liberal than it would have been otherwise. The HFC has in recent years seen its numbers and influence dwindle. The HFC experience reveals the limits of the power of a small minority of legislators. Especially if and when socialist lawmakers find themselves working under a Democratic president, they will need to be creative and strategic about how they approach fights with their own party. The efforts of the Squad — the informal grouping of young legislators including AOC, Tlaib, and others who are generally regarded as the leftmost members of the House — under the Biden administration are also instructive. In 2021, the Democrats were attempting to pass both a major infrastructure spending bill, which had broad congressional support, and Build Back Better (BBB), an expansive social welfare bill that was opposed by centrist Democratic senators Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin. The CPC, including the Squad, argued that Democratic leadership should hold a vote on the two bills together, to use the infrastructure bill as leverage to convince the centrists to vote for BBB. Ultimately, party leaders decided to split the votes — holding a vote on the infrastructure bill first, then BBB — and convinced most of the CPC, but not the Squad , to go along. The result was predictable: the infrastructure law passed, and BBB did not. Only the socialists and a few progressive allies held the line until the end, insisting correctly that splitting up the votes would likely doom the welfare bill. That’s exactly the kind of principled tactical intervention a socialist caucus can help make. Of course, in many cases, as with the Squad’s stand for BBB, the socialist minority will lose out to moderates, especially because they can’t rely even on the support of most of the CPC. But as socialists continue to grow their numbers in Congress, they will have more weight to throw around. In any case, the congressional left can’t avoid conflicts with the rest of the Democratic Party, as evidenced by party moderates’ continued denunciations of socialism and the concerted efforts of groups like the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and Third Way to discredit DSA and take down left-wing Democratic candidates. Building a Socialist Pole That fact points to one of the longer-term reasons socialists would do well to form a caucus. Given the ideological divisions among the Democrats and the unavoidable fights to come with politicians to their right, socialist legislators need their own congressional organization, one that can articulate and keep its members cohered around a distinctive political vision. Even when the socialist left can’t prevail in intraparty conflicts, being able to communicate what socialists stand for to the broader public is indispensable. A caucus will allow the Left to point to the legislators who have a demonstrated commitment to their priorities, making the case for electing more socialists and building up the broader institutional forces that can support them, like the labor movement and DSA. It will allow the socialist left to distinguish itself from the unreliable “progressives” of the CPC and other caucuses, helping it to consolidate support among the electorate. The value of a caucus will be all the greater if, as seems likely, socialists keep winning elections, and the conflict heightens. Over the last decade, the socialist left has hotly debated how to relate to the Democratic Party: whether to try to win control of it, or form a third party immediately, or tactically exploit the Democratic ballot line with the eventual goal of forming a party of our own. For now, it seems undeniable that, in most places, running on the Democratic line is the surest way to build up our forces in Congress as well as state and local offices. Yet it is clear that many in the party see socialists as an existential threat, and that in the long run this house divided against itself will not stand. There will be a struggle between those who are fighting for greater redistribution of wealth and the democratization of political and economic power, on the one hand, and those who bitterly oppose that on the other. That struggle might result in the triumph of one group or the other, staying within the confines of the Democratic Party or producing a splintering into two or more parties. Whatever happens, socialists in Congress can only benefit from starting to organize themselves for that battle now.
