articles.title: In the Midterms, America Rebuked Trump’s Authoritarianism
articles.author: Ben Burgis
articles.content: Perhaps a more competent would-be despot than Donald Trump could have pulled it off. He could have consolidated his power gradually, choosing his battles against immigrants and the Left and imagined foreign adversaries wisely and making sure he didn’t alienate his existing base of support by keeping his finger on the pulse of American sentiment and staying in tune with the struggles of average people, like the high cost of living and the exhaustion with illegal foreign wars. We’ll never know. The reaction of the bulk of the American people to the cruelty and authoritarianism they’ve seen in the last two years has been abject disgust. And they have reacted positively to the pro-worker rhetoric of Bernie Sanders and the rising Left he has inspired. Candidate after candidate seemed to have finally gotten the memo to steer clear of culture war and rhetorically emphasize affordability. What it all added up to was a “blue wave” so powerful that Republicans lost in states like Texas and South Carolina and Kansas. For those who despaired at the electorate’s handing the presidency to Trump for a second time in 2024, last night was deeply heartening: the American people decisively rejected what Trump has to offer them. First Time Farce, Second Time Tragedy Donald Trump’s first turn at the presidency was more bark than bite. He did a tremendous amount of harm, but mostly the kind of harm that a hypothetical President John McCain or President Mitt Romney would have perpetrated: he lowered taxes for rich people, slashed benefits for poor people, undermined health and safety regulations, and busted unions. There were moments where he went beyond this consensus GOP agenda, usually in the direction of performative cruelty toward immigrants, but he tended to back down in the face of judicial pushback or public outrage. Often he and the constantly rotating cast of second-rate con men he surrounded himself with seemed unsure how to wield the levers of power. There were portents of what an unleashed form of Trumpist authoritarianism might look like, particularly in his desperate attempts to overturn the results of the 2020 election. Ultimately, though, this too was a flop, and a reasonable argument could be made that Trump had simply tried to do a coarser, more “populist” version of what smarter Republicans had successfully pulled off when George W. Bush stole the 2000 election from Al Gore. The second round of Trumpism has been so much worse. Reversing Karl Marx’s formula about what happens when history repeats itself, it has been “first time farce, second time tragedy.” Trump returned to power surrounded by true believers dedicated to carrying out the president’s will, and the result has been a sustained two-year assault on liberal democracy. On his first day in office, Trump signed an executive order attempting to overturn the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of birthright citizenship. He bullied universities across the country into harsher crackdowns on students who protested the genocide in Gaza. He had legal permanent residents arrested and tried to have them deported for attending protests or writing op-eds. He had migrants, some of whom had entered legally and broken no laws, imprisoned in a Salvadoran gulag because of guesswork about what their tattoos might mean. And he sent thousands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents to occupy the city of Minneapolis as a swaggering show of force to intimidate his political opposition. When those agents murdered American citizens Alex Pretti and Renée Good, in broad daylight and on camera, the administration smeared the victims as “domestic terrorists” while their bodies were still warm. Socialists, Liberal Democracy, and “Resistance Liberalism” One important thing that “resistance liberal” types got right during and after the first Trump administration was that the president’s ambitions were more rabidly authoritarian than presidents of either party in America’s recent past. Part of what left-wing and socialist critics of “resistance liberalism” got right is that Trumpism was a natural outgrowth of that recent past, and attempts to “just get back to normal” in coalition with Never Trump Republicans very badly misread the moment. Those of us who want to fight for a better, more materially egalitarian, and more authentically democratic society understand perfectly well that liberal democracy is an indispensable starting point from which we can wage that fight. It’s what gives us the room to agitate, organize, and maneuver. So democratic socialists have stood consistently against Trumpism, as we have against previous forms of authoritarianism. Even in the early months of the administration, when many establishment Democrats didn’t seem to know what had hit them, Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were crisscrossing the country building anti-Trump enthusiasm with their Fighting Oligarchy tour, which married a defense of democracy against authoritarianism with a critique of economic inequality. This time around, many grassroots Democrats were ready to listen to that message. Enough were willing to support out-and-out socialists that a Democratic Socialists of America member is now the ( wildly popular ) mayor of the most important city in the capitalist world. And last night’s blue tidal wave more than doubled the number of socialists in Congress. Some degree of “Berniecrat”-style messaging crept into the rhetoric of Democratic candidates across the country. And Democrats in hotly contested states like Maine and Michigan openly championed substantive social democratic policies like Medicare for All. All of this represents a belated recognition that Trumpism wasn’t just a random eruption of bigotry from some toxic depth of our collective national psyche. It was a demagogic response to the material realities of a profoundly unequal and increasingly precarious society. And it’s best fought by uniting a defense of liberal democracy with a pro-worker economic message. Of course, campaign rhetoric and governance are two very different things, and the country is far from out of the woods. A profoundly dangerous authoritarian is still president — and will be for the next two years. And establishment Democrats are adept at finding creative new ways to turn even the most inspiring victories into fresh defeats. For now, though, the fact remains that the American people just handed MAGA a historically massive rebuke. That’s well worth celebrating. articles.title: Fight Against Gangster Capitalism
articles.author: Henry A. Giroux
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. With the Democratic Party’s landslide victory, a day of reckoning appears to have arrived for Trump and the far-right, white nationalist forces that have turned cruelty into a governing principle and hatred into a political language. Something has broken in the machinery of fear. The old fascist ideas, the politics of racial hatred, and the relentless assault on human dignity have encountered a moment of resistance. Too much suffering, too much misery, too much authoritarian violence. Too much blood in the streets, too many deaths, screams, and a deafening silence. Enough is enough, at least for the moment. The Trump regime has exposed some of the darkest impulses of political life, resurrecting the ghosts of a past that should have taught us where the glorification of state violence, racial cleansing, the crushing of dissent, and organized cruelty inevitably leads. Its legacy is written in the expansion of the carceral state, the staggering investment in prisons and punishment, the unleashing of masked agents of repression across the country, and the unapologetic embrace of a language of racial cleansing that strips entire populations of their humanity and destroys lives and civil liberties. Related: France’s Student Uprising: A Generation Revolts Against Capitalism Yet the celebrations now dominating liberal and mainstream media risk turning this electoral victory into an exercise in historical amnesia. Trump’s defeat is being hailed as a crushing repudiation of the far right, as though the political conditions that made his rise possible have suddenly disappeared. Missing from this triumphalist narrative is any serious reckoning with the Democratic Party’s own complicity in creating those conditions. From Clinton to Obama, Democratic administrations embraced neoliberal policies that deepened economic inequality, strengthened corporate power, weakened working-class institutions, and helped create the social and political landscape in which authoritarianism could flourish. Nor can the party's leadership escape responsibility for its support of Israel's genocidal war in Gaza, its exporting of horrendous military weapons, and its broader allegiance to a colonizing authoritarian order, sustained through violence and dispossession. A party so deeply implicated in the machinery of neoliberal capitalism cannot be entrusted with dismantling the very structures of power it has helped legitimate and preserve. For a fleeting moment, democracy may be able to breathe again. But breathing is not liberation, and an electoral victory is no substitute for dismantling the gangster capitalist order that breeds authoritarianism, feeds on human suffering, commodifies every aspect of life, and makes fascism an enduring possibility. The forces that produced Trump did not emerge overnight, nor will they disappear with an election. They are embedded in institutions that concentrate wealth, manufacture fear, normalize inequality, and transform human misery into a source of profit and political power. Trump may be defeated at the ballot box, but Trumpism cannot be defeated without confronting the economic, political, and cultural foundations of a system that turns greed into virtue, cruelty into policy, racism into a badge of honor, and human disposability into a governing principle. Related: When Words Become Weapons of Racial Terror Unless those foundations are dismantled, the nightmare will return, perhaps wearing a different mask. The serpent's egg, to invoke the haunting metaphor associated with Ingmar Bergman, has not been destroyed. It lies beneath the surface of seemingly democratic societies, nourished by the dark and volatile forces of a capitalist order that breeds inequality, authoritarianism, and organized cruelty. Brecht understood that fascism could not be confronted without exposing the capitalist relations of power that give rise to it. The serpent's egg remains embedded in the political, economic, and cultural machinery of gangster capitalism, waiting for the conditions under which it can hatch again. Fascism may suffer an electoral defeat, but the serpent survives, sustained by the very system that gave it life. There is another historical lesson that cannot be buried beneath the celebrations of an electoral victory: the need to recover the spirit of the Nuremberg trials. Nuremberg established a principle that must never be forgotten those who organize, authorize, and carry out state crimes cannot hide behind the authority of government or the excuse of following orders. The Trump regime has left behind a record of actions demanding criminal investigation, from the killing of people aboard boats in international waters, including attacks that legal experts have warned may constitute war crimes, to the abduction, imprisonment, and deportation of people in violation of fundamental rights and due process. The Democratic Party has a responsibility to ensure that these abuses are investigated and that those responsible, from Pete Hegseth to Stephen Miller and others who directed or enabled such policies, are held accountable wherever the evidence establishes criminal responsibility. There can be no reconciliation purchased at the expense of justice, no national healing built on organized forgetting, and no democratic renewal that grants impunity to those who turned the machinery of the state into an instrument of terror. The lesson of Nuremberg is not that history repeats itself in identical forms, but that crimes committed under the cover of state power must be exposed, judged, and punished through the rule of law. Without accountability, the promise of an electoral victory in the spirit of reviving democratic values and policies becomes another empty slogan, and the forces of authoritarian violence are given permission to return. The possibility of genuine transformation will not emerge from the exhausted leadership of a Democratic Party unwilling to break with the capitalist order it serves. It will emerge from the streets, from organized workers, from young people refusing to be written out of history, and from collective struggles that reject the politics of fear, austerity, racial hatred, and disposability. Elections may interrupt the march toward authoritarianism—a crucial pedagogical function-- but they cannot abolish the conditions-the myriad economic, political, and cultural forces-that make fascism possible. The task now is to turn this moment of resistance into a sustained struggle against the structures of power that have made democracy increasingly subordinate to wealth, militarism, and corporate domination. The future cannot be entrusted to political elites in suites, who promise to rescue democracy while preserving the economic order that is destroying it. The struggle is not simply to defeat one authoritarian leader, but to dismantle a system that makes authoritarianism possible and to build a world in which justice, equality, collective freedom, and human dignity become the foundations of democratic life.

articles.title: Last Night’s Victories Were Made Possible by Zohran Mamdani
articles.author: Corey Robin
articles.content: If there’s one person who saw yesterday’s repudiation of the right coming long before everyone else did, it’s Zohran Mamdani. In one way or another, he and the movement that created him are the architects of the Democrats’ victory. Two years ago, the day after the 2024 election, the mood was grim; the future was bleak. Nobody saw the possibility for regrouping. What did Mamdani do? Just one week after Donald Trump’s victory, he went out and interviewed Trump voters all across the city. He spoke to white, black, brown, Muslim, Asian, but above all working-class men and women and, above all, in the Bronx and Queens. Everyone now thinks of Mamdani’s victory a year later, first in the primary and then in the general election, as a foregone conclusion, a New York thing that had no meaning beyond New York. It wasn’t. The reason it wasn’t is that Mamdani understood something no one else understood: Trump voters had their reasons for going for Trump, and those reasons could be explained and understood. Not the hard-bitten right-winger, mind you, but the people who put Trump over the top. That reason was economic. Mamdani saw that, and he gave it a name: affordability. And lo and behold, what did one Texas voter, who’s voted Republican all his life, say last night about how and why he voted for the Democrats for the first time? No one can afford anything anymore. Our water and air is the dirtiest and our education is horrible. Mamdani spoke to that sentiment with his use of the term “affordability.” It’s not just a strictly economic word; as this Texas voter suggests, it’s almost a spiritual term, a sense of the enshittification of life, the grinding worsening of material and therefore cultural conditions. Water is dirty; education is horrible; it’s all going to shit. That’s what Mamdani spoke to, and he said, “We can do something about that.” So many politicians now use that word “affordability” that we forget it was Mamdani who, less than two years ago, made that the word. And what every other Democratic politician across the United States, whether they’re Democratic Socialists of America or not, saw is that those Trump voters, those swing Trump voters, are gettable — if you can speak about the economic and cultural catastrophe that has been visited upon ordinary citizens. Whether we’re talking about the Latino men who shifted right toward Trump along the border in Texas or the farmers in the Midwest who’ve voted Republican their whole lives till yesterday, or the Solid South. Look at the voters who shifted from Republican to Democrat yesterday and the demographic trends. Remember those young people who voted Trump and were declared lost for a generation to the tradwives and the manosphere? They saw the largest shift left of any demographic group. Voters eighteen to twenty-nine years old saw a 32-point shift to the left. White noncollege voters, which is how this addled nation codes “white working class,” saw a 14-point shift to the left. Latino voters saw a 28-point shift to the left. It took a Muslim socialist, born in Uganda, raised in New York City, to give the American heartland a new kind of language to wage political battle against the Right. Just as it was Jewish socialists a century ago, many of them immigrants and raised in New York City, who gave America during the 1930s and 1940s, in politics and culture, in the wake of one of the first anti-immigrant backlashes the country had ever seen, a new language for itself. articles.title: The Donald Trump Era in American Politics Is Ending
articles.author: Paul Heideman
articles.content: The American people delivered an absolute rout against Donald Trump and the GOP last night. Here are five takeaways from the midterm results: 1. Trump Owns This Defeat Everything about this defeat points to a different way Donald Trump has weakened the Republican Party. In Texas and South Carolina, he pushed his preferred candidates, Ken Paxton and Darline Graham, for the Senate above the first choices of the state parties. Both were terrible candidates and terrible campaigners who made the Democrats’ job vastly easier. In Florida, he pushed an aggressive gerrymander that energized Democratic voters while failing to net any additional seats for Republicans. Nationwide, the nakedly criminal war on Iran combined with his refusal to even humor voters’ anger at the cost of living weighed down every Republican in the country. Over the last few weeks, Trump implored voters to pretend he was on the ticket. They followed his advice. 2. Billionaire Money Wasn’t Enough One reason Trump and the rest of the party felt empowered to simply ignore clear signs from the electorate was their massive financial advantage. A few dozen billionaires, including Elon Musk, Miriam Adelson, the Winklevoss brothers, and Ken Griffin, poured truly staggering amounts of money into Republican super PACs. Trump’s personal super PAC, MAGA, Inc., had over $400 million in its account. That was more money than the Democratic Senate super PAC, House super PAC, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, and Democratic National Committee combined . Most of the Republican financial advantage was spent on the Senate, where the GOP outspent Democrats by about 50 percent. Republicans expected to be able to use this golden hoard to simply crush Democrats in states like Texas. It wasn’t nearly enough — a fact that should be heartening to anyone dismayed about the undemocratic effects of big money in politics. 3. The Knives Are Going to Come Out for Trump Because of the previous two points, Republican politicians are going to turn on Trump quickly. The writing is on the wall for 2028. There is no reason to think that a president whose connection to reality is visibly attenuating with each passing week will be able to turn his popularity around in the next two years. Any Republican with ambitions for the future will be racing to create distance between themselves and the administration. The few Republicans who openly opposed Trump in the last few years, like Ron DeSantis , are already blaming Trump for the defeat and calling for a new direction for the party. Determining that direction will be a messy, conflictual process, with open conflict among different elements of the party. But with every passing day, there will be fewer and fewer reasons for members of the party to continue their obeisance to Trump. 4. Democrats Won the Biggest Overall Congressional Majority for Either Party Since the GOP in 2014 The size of the Democratic majority is striking. As of Wednesday morning, most projections have the Democrats winning about 245 seats in the House, and fifty-four or fifty-five seats in the Senate. This puts the Democrats in a similar position to the Republicans in 2014, when the GOP expanded on its majority in the House and finally recaptured the Senate from the Democrats. Since the Trump era began, no party has had majorities of this size in both the House and the Senate. In both the House and the Senate, this vastly decreases the leverage available to small minorities of the caucuses. In the Senate, John Fetterman will not be able to block progressive legislation the way Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema were during the Biden administration. Similarly, in the House, even the expanded team of socialist legislators will not come close to providing the margin of victory for the Democratic majority. In this context, Democratic politics will likely reflect the center of gravity of the caucus in each chamber, rather than the power of a few legislators holding strategic veto points. 5. The Left Is Continuing to Rise Across the country, this was a fantastic night for the Left. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates, as expected, won their general elections in places like New York, Colorado, and Michigan. Moreover, DSA candidates won election to the state house in close races in Kentucky and Florida. Candidates like Troy Jackson and Abdul El-Sayed, who are often associated with DSA despite not being members, also won races that were widely seen as tests for the progressive wing of the Democratic Party. Angie Nixon, a DSA member who won an upset victory in her primary for Florida’s senate seat, came within a few points of winning in a state most liberals had written off as irredeemably red. Exit polls, meanwhile, showed that three times as many young voters described themselves as democratic socialists as MAGA. DSA’s project has clearly not hit its ceiling yet, and these results show that it is time to take the fight to new battlegrounds. articles.title: UAW Members Successfully Oust Commissioner Responsible for 8-Month Strike in Lorain County, Ohio
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: After months of organizing that began in July, the UAW has helped oust Lorain County Commissioner Jeff Riddell, who refused to settle a fair contract with striking Lorain County Job and Family Services workers. Frustrated by his resistance to good-faith negotiations, the union shifted its fight from the bargaining table to the voting booth, reaching ten thousand doors of UAW members across Lorain County to turn out the vote for Riddell’s opponent, Carolyn White. “Our members put in the work to ensure elected officials are held accountable to the voters they serve,” said UAW Region 2B Director Dave Green. “UAW members stayed focused on making sure county, state, and federal governments work to make people’s lives better, not harder. When elected officials fail working people, UAW members have shown they will hold them accountable at the ballot box.” The UAW’s electoral program mobilized 150 UAW members and volunteers to knock on thousands of doors and make tens of thousands of phone calls to union members in Elyria, North Ridgeville, Avon, Vermilion, Oberlin, Wellington, Grafton, and Sheffield in Lorain County. Since February 18, UAW Local 2192 members at Lorain County Job and Family Services have been on strike after county commissioners, including Riddell, refused to approve the $1-per-hour raises workers need to keep up with today’s affordability crisis. “This is absolute proof: voters in Lorain County are sick of corrupt elected officials like Jeff Riddell who are bad at their jobs,” said UAW Local 2192 bargaining committee chair and case worker on strike at Job and Family Services. “We’re facing too much of an affordability crisis that all of us are hurt by. Our strike has been the clearest example of how important it is to elect people who represent the interests of the working class.” Riddell’s refusal to reach a fair agreement with public service workers prolonged Lorain County’s public service crisis, extending what is already the longest public-sector strike in Ohio history and putting it just weeks away from becoming the longest in U.S. history. UAW canvassers knocking on doors across Lorain County came from workplaces throughout the area represented by the union. Even while on strike during the week, UAW Local 2192 members volunteered on Saturdays, joining large-scale canvass efforts to talk with fellow UAW members and their families about why Commissioner Jeff Riddell needed to be ousted on November 3.

articles.title: National Park Signs
articles.author: Robert Ito
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In January, park rangers removed 34 interpretive panels from a slavery exhibit at Independence National Historical Park in Philadelphia. The signs, which described the lives of the nine people George Washington enslaved at the presidential residence there, were unceremoniously taken down — in some cases leaving the dried glue in place — to comply with President Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14253 , titled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” The order calls for the removal of signs that “inappropriately disparage Americans past or living” from the country’s national parks. Apparently, telling visitors about our first president’s slaves ran afoul of that. When Trump issued the order in March 2025, Molly Blake, a social sciences librarian at the University of Minnesota, worried about the information that might be lost as a result. She began talking with colleagues at the university, including Jenny McBurney, a government publications librarian, about what they could do. Even if they couldn’t stop park rangers from tearing down the signs, maybe they could archive them for posterity. Within a few months, they would launch Save Our Signs , a nationwide effort to preserve what the government was trying to erase. Blake and McBurney couldn’t go to all 63 national parks, of course, let alone the hundreds of historic monuments and sites overseen by the National Park Service. “We knew we had to get the public involved,” Blake said, so they invited parkgoers to photograph signs to be recorded in an online archive. The response has been overwhelming. To date, members of the public have sent Save Our Signs more than 17,000 photos shot at 428 sites, from Ellis Island and the Japanese American internment camp at Manzanar to monuments dedicated to the memory of Emmett Till , whose killing helped spark the Civil Rights Movement. They’ve also sent reports and photos from parks where the signs have already been removed, which become part of the archive’s “Censorship Tracker.” “The folks that we hear from are saying things like they love our parks, they support our parks, they want to maintain the really high-quality educational materials they’re seeing there,” McBurney said. “They want us to remember our history, the good and the bad.” A Daunting Task Even for the combined forces of the American public, however, there are a lot of parks and land to cover: more than 85 million acres across 50 states. And nobody knows where the government might strike next. “They’re not hiding it,” said Alan Spears, senior director of cultural resources at the National Parks Conservation Association. “They’re also probably not putting out press releases saying that this stuff has happened. You can just show up on Monday or Tuesday of this past week, [and] the signs are gone.” Because of the uncertainty, SOS encourages parkgoers to photograph everything. “One of the signs that was removed just noted that it’s a good idea to refill your water bottle because it’s better for the environment than using plastic,” Blake said. “I wouldn’t have guessed that that would have been targeted, but it was.” Since the order was issued, park employees have removed or modified more than 100 signs at 41 National Park Service sites, from California’s Muir Woods National Monument (for mentioning climate change and the park founders’ connections to anti-immigrant policies) to Wyoming’s Grand Teton National Park (for calling attention to explorer Gustavus Cheyney Doane’s participation in a massacre of more than 150 Indigenous people). Monitoring all those signs is as daunting for the Interior Department, which includes the Park Service, as it is for SOS. The department relies on park rangers and other employees at each site, instructing them to look for signs that might not be doing an acceptable job of reminding parkgoers of this country’s “unmatched record of advancing liberty, prosperity, and human flourishing,” as Trump’s order puts it. Park staff are expected to remove or alter such signs within 120 days of the executive order. Related: This L.A. Museum Stands Up to Trump’s Whitewashing, Vowing to ‘Scrub Nothing’ Snitch Signs A confidential Park Service database, leaked in March and containing internal communications among park staffers, showed rangers wrestling with difficult questions about what exactly the order requires. Did signage about the return of California condors from near-extinction disparage hunters? one ranger asked. Another wondered whether signs about graffiti at Utah’s Arches National Park violated the directive to emphasize the park’s “natural beauty.” For SOS, the leak provided a list of parks that might be targeted for sign removals if they hadn’t been already. “Right now, we have on our website a map of parks that, based on the leaked dataset of what might be targeted, are parks that are priorities for us,” Blake said. “It was called out on this leaked spreadsheet as a place that there might be censorship happening. We really want more photos there.” One of the challenges for Save Our Signs is the ambiguity of Trump’s order as well as Secretarial Order 3431 , which Interior Secretary Doug Burgum issued to implement the executive order. Consider the orders’ ban on “inappropriate disparagement” of Americans. Is it OK for signage at a Till site to disparage the men who tortured and lynched him? Can park signs at civil rights monuments in Birmingham, Alabama, and Little Rock, Arkansas, disparage the white supremacists who opposed the Civil Rights Movement? “Inappropriate disparagement” of Americans is “a really confusing turn of phrase,” McBurney said. “Especially in the early days, nobody knew what that meant.” The secretarial order also requires parks to post notices telling visitors how to report supposed violations, an effort that has largely been a bust. The QR-code-enabled notices, prescribed in a section of Burgum’s order titled “Encouraging Public Participation,” were soon dubbed “snitch signs” by detractors, thousands of whom submitted sarcastic comments and jabs at the Trump administration. “There are some people who reported, ‘I think there needs to be more about Indigenous history here,’” Blake said. Legal Conflicts The watchdog group Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (PEER) filed a Freedom of Information Act request last year to find out how the executive order was being implemented. The Interior Department never responded, so PEER sued to get the records in June. Tony Irish, a longtime Interior attorney who left the department last year and joined PEER in May, said, “There’s a number of terms [in the order] that, even for me, with my background in Interior programs, isn’t clear.” He wonders how these orders might run afoul of federal law, including the National Park Service Organic Act of 1916, which created the service, and the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. “There’s other sites, particularly ones like Little Big Horn, where Congress has specifically directed the agency to provide a viewpoint from the Native American tribes that were impacted by the events there,” Irish said. It’s not just Park Service signs that are being removed and altered. Trump’s order calls for the removal of offending signs throughout all 500 million acres of Interior Department lands, comprising roughly one-fifth of the country. Park Service sites are getting most of the attention because Americans are more inclined to visit them, Irish said, but the Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Land Management oversee even more acreage. PEER is suing the department for information about the order’s impact on those lands too. There have been impacts on wildlife refuges and the Bureau of Land Management, Irish said. “Part of why we want to get these records is to see just to what extent.” Insidious Alterations Little is known about the fate of many of the lost signs. When a district court judge told the Trump administration to provide an inventory of removed materials, the partial list from the Interior Department included 18 items that had been “discarded.” Few parks employees are inclined to talk about where the old signs might be, let alone which others are slated for removal, Irish said. “We’ve seen … circumstances where employees have made their personal feelings known that have led to swift reactions from the department,” he said. “So I would suspect there is some fear of being open about that.” Some of the replacement signs sanitize or dilute the history laid out in the originals in ways that aren’t immediately obvious. “These are really insidious,” said Save Our Signs’ Blake. “The differences are really subtle. In one case, a sign about Black soldiers during the Civil War, a reference to the fact that the military remained segregated until after World War II, that sentence was quietly taken out. So you could read something like that and not realize this has been censored.” This whitewashing of history at park sites reverses decades of progress at the national parks, Spears said. “We spent the last 30 years trying to raise up some of these untold stories so that we can have a better understanding of the contributions that all of us have made,” she said. Spears called the current shift “disheartening and anger-inducing.” Save Our Signs continues to document the loss as signs across the country continue to come down. Blake said the effort is capturing an important moment in our history when an accurate telling of our past is itself under attack. “Best-case scenario, the signs that have been censored will go back up, and this will be a way to study what happened,” she said. “Worst-case scenario, if this censorship continues, we want to be documenting it so that people can see what has been changed.” Capital & Main

articles.title: Giving Community Photos a Second Life
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A neighborhood organization may have years of photographs and still struggle to find a suitable picture for its next announcement. A street-fair photo is too small for print, a workshop picture has harsh lighting, and another carries last year's event date. For groups that run on volunteer time and limited budgets, taking new photographs for every newsletter or campaign is rarely practical. Thoughtful editing can make existing material useful again. Begin with the purpose of the picture Before editing anything, decide what the audience needs from the image. An event announcement should tell people what kind of gathering to expect. A report on a neighborhood project may need to show who participated and what actually happened. An archival photograph accompanying a local history piece has a different obligation: its details are part of the record. Those distinctions affect even ordinary choices. Brightening a dim meeting-room photograph may help readers see the participants. Replacing the room with an imaginary, more attractive venue could mislead them. Likewise, a tighter crop may improve a social post, but it could exclude the volunteers whose work the organization intended to recognize. It helps to keep an untouched original and write down the intended use before opening an editor. That small habit makes later decisions easier. Edit one problem at a time Natural-language editing is useful for volunteers who know what they want changed but have little experience with traditional photo software. In Pixlio's AI image editor , someone can upload a reference photo, describe the change, choose a supported model and review the result. The edited image can then become the starting point for another revision. A practical instruction could be: "Reduce the yellow cast from the indoor lighting and brighten the faces slightly. Keep the people, posters and room arrangement unchanged." It gives the editor a specific job and sets boundaries. Compare the result with the original before using it, paying particular attention to faces, printed signs and small objects that automated edits sometimes alter. There is no need to solve every issue in one prompt. A photo intended for a website banner might need a different crop after its lighting is corrected. The workspace also supports creating an image from text, useful when an organization needs an illustration or concept graphic rather than a photograph of something that happened. Choose tools that suit the actual task Pixlio is also an AI image creative studio with specialized tools for recurring jobs. Its AI Photo Restoration tool can help with scanned photographs showing scratches, fading or weak color. For a neighborhood anniversary display, that may be a reasonable way to make old pictures easier to view. Restoration should still be checked against the scan, especially where faces or historical details are unclear. The Image Text Remover is useful when an image has an outdated digital caption or date overlaid on it and the group wants to reuse the underlying photograph. Keep a copy with the original wording, and avoid treating text on real-world signs as disposable. An Image Upscaler can prepare a small image for a larger layout, though added sharpness cannot recover information that was never captured by the camera. After an initial edit, Pixlio lets users carry the selected image into a separate upscaling or other specialized process without starting again from a blank upload. Each step still deserves a fresh review. Leave room for trust Community organizations depend on people recognizing themselves and their neighborhoods in the material they publish. Ask permission when a recognizable person's image is being reused in a new context, particularly for promotional campaigns. If an image comes from an earlier event, label it accordingly rather than letting readers assume it shows the upcoming gathering. AI-generated illustrations can work well for ideas that have no documentary photograph, such as a proposed garden or an imagined future streetscape. Describe them as concepts. For images presented as evidence of a completed project or an actual turnout, ordinary accuracy is more important than visual polish. A good final check is to ask someone unfamiliar with the editing process what they believe the picture shows. If their answer differs from what took place, revisit the edit or improve the caption. A mistaken event label or altered sign is easier to correct before the picture reaches a flyer or newsletter.
